articles.title_orig: Trump turns on Salazar after Florida Republican challenges his immigration crackdown
articles.title_zh: Trump turns on Salazar after Florida Republican challenges his immigration crackdown
articles.content_orig:
Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, R-Florida, has made waves by publicly breaking with President Donald Trump over immigration.
"Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far," Salazar says in a new campaign ad . "The same Hispanics that helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today."
In 2024, voters broadly trusted Republicans to handle illegal immigration. Through incompetence and cruelty, the Trump administration has lost that goodwill. The last election showed Republicans have a path forward on immigration. But to take it, they need to ditch the cruel memes and aggressive tactics that have plagued Trump's second term.
Salazar is right: Hispanics were a major part of Trump's 2024 victory. According to Pew Research Center, the president nearly tied former Vice President Kamala Harris among Hispanic voters, a group former President Joe Biden won by 25 percentage points in 2020.
Since then, Trump's gains among Hispanics have evaporated. In February 2025, according to Pew , 93% of Hispanics who voted for Trump approved of the job he was doing. By April of this year, just 66% did. Over the same stretch, his approval among all Hispanic adults fell from 36% to 22%, while among non-Hispanic adults, it slipped from 49% to 37%.
The drop in support can be attributed largely to the administration's mishandling of immigration.
The loudest headlines came out of Operation Metro Surge, the enforcement campaign that flooded Minneapolis with more than 3,000 federal agents last winter. The surge was driven more by political optics than by any strategic need, and it ended with Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Border Patrol agents shooting and killing two U.S. citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti.
Worse yet, administration officials then smeared Pretti . White House advisor Stephen Miller called him a "domestic terrorist," and the Department of Homeland Security claimed he "wanted to do maximum damage and massacre law enforcement." Bystander video showed he never drew his holstered pistol, which he was licensed to carry. Americans noticed: 61% of voters told Quinnipiac University pollsters that the administration had not given an honest account of the shooting.
Previously: We need to change the way we talk about the ICE shooting | Opinion
By mid-February, Americans opposed ICE's tactics 62% to 31%, according to an ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll. The backlash presumably helped cost Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem her job.
Since Noem's firing, ICE has largely faded from the headlines, as DHS Sec. Markwayne Mullin has worked to keep the agency out of the spotlight. That changed Sept. 20, when an ICE officer in Austin shot and wounded Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, a Venezuelan man with a deportation order who had fled a vehicle stop. The facts are still unclear, and there is no ICE body-camera footage of the shooting. After Minneapolis, Americans have little reason to give the administration the benefit of the doubt.

Beyond the heated environment it needlessly created in Minnesota, the administration has driven support away with its messaging.
Throughout Trump's second term, official government social media accounts have churned out memes , many of them about immigration. The White House posted a Studio Ghibli-style cartoon of a convicted drug trafficker weeping as she was arrested and has promised that "the memes will continue." Other posts have included mock travel ads for deportation flights, and the administration has co-opted endless TikTok memes and audio trends to celebrate deportations.
All of it undercuts the administration's posture on such a serious matter. Nobody has ever been won over to a policy by a cartoon of a crying deportee, criminal or not. All it does is deepen the divide.
Austin ICE shooting proves we've lost ability to wait for facts | Opinion
Frustration with Democrats' failures at the border handed Republicans an opening in 2024. Voters trusted Trump over Harris on immigration 51% to 38%. Republicans have since squandered that advantage, but the path to a sensible immigration policy isn't closed.
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer shot and injured a man in North Austin on Sept. 20, officials say.
The man who was injured in the shooting was identified as Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, of Venezuela, by Austin immigration lawyer Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, who said she was hired to represent him.
The incident was followed by a swift reaction from elected officials, as the public protested the latest shooting involving federal officers in the United States this year.
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer shot and injured a man in North Austin on Sept. 20, officials say.
The man who was injured in the shooting was identified as Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, of Venezuela, by Austin immigration lawyer Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, who said she was hired to represent him.
Americans still draw a line between securing the border and Trump's broader crackdown. In a New York Times/Siena College poll in January, roughly half of voters approved of his handling of the border, while they were split on deportations and a clear majority said ICE had "gone too far." That gap shows sensible border policy still has broad support, despite the administration's spectacle of mismanagement and cruelty.
Trump's inroads with Hispanic voters in 2024 were thought to signal a new Republican coalition, and they showed that these voters could back a more conservative immigration policy. Those gains have all but vanished. What looked like a lasting Republican asset has become a serious liability heading into the midterms.
To win back their advantage on immigration, Republicans need to ditch the cruelty. The memes, ICE's aggressive tactics and the general callousness have soured Americans on policies that should command popular support for years to come.
Lawmakers like Salazar may be breaking with Trump for electoral reasons. But if they win in November, they will be the ones building the Republican Party's next approach to immigration. That approach should press Democrats on their weaknesses on the issue, without the cruelty that has defined Trump's second term.

articles.title_orig: Iowa vs Michigan recap: Iowa wins with last-second TD, 20-19
articles.title_zh: Iowa vs Michigan recap: Iowa wins with last-second TD, 20-19
articles.content_orig:
Michigan got a taste of its own medicine on Saturday at the Big House.
The Wolverines, who were the beneficiaries of a controversial last-second win in their season opener, were victimized in the final plays of a devastating 20-19 loss to rival Iowa.
On the penultimate play of Iowa’s game-winning drive, Hawkeyes quarterback Hank Brown connected with receiver Addison Ostrenga to get into the red zone — but with just two seconds on the clock, time was going to run out before the offense could get another play off.
Unreal play to keep Iowa in it! pic.twitter.com/l6EY5M10t6
Then Iowa was handed a lifeline.
Michigan defensive end John Henry Daley went down with an injury during the play, meaning that the game clock halted at two seconds, giving Iowa another crack to score a game-winning touchdown.
And the Hawkeyes took full advantage, with Brown finding wideout Reece Vander Zee in the corner of the end zone for a 16-yard game-winning score.
The extra time on the clock comes with a bit of irony, as the Wolverines controversially defeated Western Michigan , 13-12, in their Week 1 win after officials awarded Michigan an extra second because a defender touched the ball with a second left on the stadium clock on the Wolverines’ initial Hail Mary attempt.
Given a second chance, Michigan quarterback Bryce Underwood heaved a deep ball caught in the end zone by JJ Buchanan to seal the 13-12 win, which caused an uproar across college football.
On Saturday, however, it was Michigan on the receiving end as Iowa scored 13 unanswered points in the fourth quarter.
“One thing about these guys is that they don’t quit,” Hawkeyes head coach Kirk Ferentz said in a postgame interview. “It wasn’t perfect, but they don’t give up.”
The win is Iowa’s first victory over a ranked Big Ten opponent since 2021, snapping a nine-game losing streak against such teams.
“Never won like this, so it’s what we’ll all remember,” Ferentz added.
“We’ll enjoy the heck out of it tonight, and back to work tomorrow.”

articles.title_orig: Trump Administration Plans to Gut Clean Car Rules
articles.title_zh: Trump Administration Plans to Gut Clean Car Rules
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump on Saturday said he approved new fuel economy standards , reversing former President Joe Biden's stricter policies meant to fuel electric vehicle adoption.
Since the Corporate Average Fuel Economy, or CAFE, standards were established in 1975, they have been periodically updated, typically to make vehicles more efficient. Under former President Joe Biden's standards , automakers would have had to increase the fuel efficiency of their passenger cars and light trucks to roughly 50 miles per gallon by 2031. The stricter standards were designed to incentivize electric vehicle production and sales in the U.S.
Trump presented the policy change as a boon for both automakers and consumers, though the final standards have not yet been publicly detailed.
"These new Standards will take the waste out of building cars in America. That means LOWER PRICES, saving families thousands on a new, beautiful, and safe car — Far better than the Environmental Monsters that we were building heretofore," he wrote in the Truth Social post . "Every Manufacturer, from General Motors to Ford to Stellantis, has called me wanting to build here, and now they can!"
The regulatory change would fulfill a campaign promise from Trump to rescind policies that encouraged or incentivized electric vehicles.
It is unclear what the final fuel economy standards will be, although Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy previously said that they would be sharply lower than the Biden-era policies.
Weaker fuel economy standards mean that automakers can produce more pickup trucks and SUVs, which are much more profitable than smaller cars but have worse gas mileage. Electric vehicles also become much less attractive to automakers, although some companies, like General Motors , have said that they will still make them.

Surf City, New Jersey, was among coastal communities flooded
Tens of millions of people across the north-eastern US are in the path of a powerful storm bringing coastal flooding, power cuts, travel chaos and cancelled stadium events.
The so-called nor'easter is bringing "dangerous coastal flooding and beach conditions, strong winds and heavy rainfall" to areas including New York City and Boston on Saturday, the US National Weather Service (NWS) said.
States of emergency have been declared in New York and New Jersey, both of which faced a coastal deluge in some areas. Rain and strong winds are forecast from Virginia to Maine.
Ed Sheeran's much-awaited Boston concert was among events called off due to the weather.
Residents on kayaks in a Beach Haven West, New Jersey, neighbourhood
The nor'easter caused widespread power cuts. More than 100,000 households, nearly all in the northeast US, have lost electricity, according to tracker PowerOutage.
The Federal Aviation Administration recommended air passengers check with airlines about their flight status. More than 2,400 flights have been delayed and another 1,199 grounded, according to FlightAware.
Saturday's full moon is projected to worsen coastal flooding. Streets and homes were inundated with floodwater in the coastal New Jersey communities of Surf City and Manasquan on Saturday.
"I urge all New Jerseyans to take this storm seriously, stay alert and follow local guidance," Governor Mikie Sherrill said.
Streets and homes were inundated with floodwater in coastal parts of New Jersey
Flights have been delayed or cancelled due to the storm
NWS said in its alert: "Prepare immediately for significant inundation in low-lying areas near the shore, including roads underwater and impacts to homes and businesses."
In New York, officials are warning of wind gusts of up to 55mph (86km/h) throughout the weekend, leading to downed trees and power lines.
"Don't travel if you don't have to," NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani told residents in a video message. "Do not drive or walk through floodwater."
In the Boston area, the Red Sox moved the last game in their series against the Chicago Cubs to Sunday afternoon in Florida.
Waves pounded the coast in Massachusetts
A professional football match between Red Bull New York and St Louis City SC was also cancelled.
Nor is the Global Citizen Festival concert in New York City's Central Park, which was to be headlined by Lauryn Hill, Wyclef Jean and John Legend, going ahead.
Sheeran's concert at the Gillette Stadium in the Boston area was cancelled for safety reasons, the venue said.

articles.title_orig: Iran War Updates: Trump rejects 7-day plan to reopen Strait of Hormuz
articles.title_zh: Iran War Updates: Trump rejects 7-day plan to reopen Strait of Hormuz
articles.content_orig:
Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi called at the United Nations Saturday for "self-restraint" from all sides in the Middle East war, while stressing that Muscat was ready to mediate.
"We call upon all parties concerned to settle their outstanding disputes through pursuing a policy of self-restraint and foresight, and through engaging in dialog to reach consensual, political solutions and sustainable understandings for the benefit of all," Albusaidi said, addressing world leaders gathered in New York.
"Oman once again reaffirms its steadfast commitment to continuing its efforts aimed at safeguarding navigation in the Strait of Hormuz ... We also call upon all parties to cooperate with Oman in these efforts."
Oman sits across the Strait of Hormuz from Iran, and ships seeking to skirt Tehran's restrictions have recently been taking a route that hugs the Omani coast.
Saudi Arabia warned U.N. members Saturday that attempts to block Middle East waterways are a threat to global energy security and demanded the international community do more to defend freedom of navigation.
"The international community has been absent from assuming its responsibilities in confronting all that threatens international peace and security," Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan told the United Nations General Assembly.
"The kingdom stresses the importance of guaranteeing the protection of freedom of navigation in all international waterways, foremost among them the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden," he said.
The minister further demanded the return of conditions in the Strait of Hormuz to what they were before Feb. 28, without imposing any fees or taxes.
"The kingdom rejects any party's use of these vital passages as a tool for pressure, threat, or harm to the interests of states, in a manner consistent with international law and relevant United Nations resolutions," he said.
Bin Farhan was speaking shortly after President Trump had rejected an Iranian proposal of a deal to reopen Hormuz, in exchange for — among other conditions — a Middle East ceasefire and the release of frozen Iranian assets.
Reopening the Strait of Hormuz has been the focal point of much of the negotiations, but the Saudis have been facing increased difficulties transporting oil due to the Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen effectively closing the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the southern exit to the Red Sea, through targeting Saudi-flagged tankers and attacks on the East-West pipeline through inland Saudi Arabia.
As the world deals with decreasing oil supplies and increasing prices, President Trump asked his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping to increase petroleum production in his country, according to the White House.
The White House provided a fact sheet following Mr. Trump's meeting with Xi for a state visit this week that highlights "President Trump urged President Xi to increase production of refined petroleum products to stabilize global supply."
The war with Iran, and its spread to Saudi Arabia, has tightened global energy supplies even as the U.S. has worked to escort tankers out of the Persian Gulf. Mr. Trump said earlier Saturday that 29 vessels had been guided out of the Strait of Hormuz under military supervision.
But the supply of oil and natural gas have still suffered compared to prewar levels. And the revived fighting between the Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government has now led to the closure of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Saudi-flagged oil tankers.
Brent crude, the international standard, closed the week at $104 a barrel, the same as it began the week, despite rising to $108 on Thursday.
Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Russia is ready to help stabilize the situation in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Gulf region, as the U.S.-Iran conflict drags on.
"We need trust in the relationships between the Gulf states, the Arab states and Iran. We need stable regional architecture," Lavrov told leaders Saturday at the U.N. General Assembly.
"Russia, together with other responsible states, stands ready to constructively contribute to stabilizing this strategically important region."
Lavrov did not elaborate on how Russia would provide assistance to end the conflict spreading across the Middle East.
Russia has long been an ally of Iran. Iran provided Shahed drones to Russia for its own invasion of Ukraine. Russia in turn has reportedly assisted Iran with satellite coordination to target U.S. forces in the region.
The Israeli army destroyed an alleged Hezbollah weapons storage facility in southern Lebanon on Saturday.
"Earlier today (Saturday), the IDF struck a weapons storage facility belonging to the Hezbollah terrorist organization in the Sejoud area of southern Lebanon," the IDF said in a statement. "The strike was carried out to remove a threat: the facility stored weapons that were used to target IDF soldiers operating in the Security Zone."
The so-called "security zone" is an area of southern Lebanon set up by Israel that reaches about 6 or 7 miles into the country from the northern Israeli border.
Israel and Hezbollah have signed several short-term ceasefires, mostly recently in late June, but they have all been punctuated by violations from both sides. Deals signed between Israel and the Lebanese government, including the trilateral agreement brokered by the U.S., have each been rejected by Hezbollah.
President Trump has rejected the latest proposal from Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in seven days and launch in-depth negotiations to end the war.
"I'm rejecting their deal," Mr. Trump told reporters while leaving the White House on Saturday to travel to Tennessee. "They want to make a deal where they open the strait immediately because they are losing so badly. You don't see that in the fake news. We're winning tremendously, we have total control of the Hormuz Strait, massive amounts of oil are coming out of the Hormuz Strait, last night we had 29 ships come out."
"They want to make a deal," he continued. "I think that's fine, I like making a deal too. But that deal [they offered] would not be acceptable."
Both the U.S. and Iran had expressed optimism over talks held in New York during the U.N. General Assembly, though they were short on details of what was discussed. Mr. Trump did not attend the talks directly, but his son-in-law, Jared Kushner, and special envoy Steve Witkoff were involved in the negotiations with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.
The deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz was reportedly similar to the Islamabad memorandum signed in June, including ending the blockade, allowing Iranian oil sales and halting fighting in every Middle East theater. The U.S. disputed Iran's interpretation of the MOU over who controlled traffic in the strait and the deal fell apart by July.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian had told CBS News' Margaret Brennan on Friday that his country was standing at the ready to implement the new deal.
"If this message reaches the president of the United States, or the interviewers and those involved in the discussions, naturally the process will begin from the very day they accept it," he said.
China pushed back against the United States in its speech at the U.N. General Assembly on Saturday, saying sovereignty of countries in the Gulf should be respected.
Vice President Han Zheng did not mention the U.S. by name in his remarks.
The comments stood in sharp contrast to the friendship on display earlier this week at the White House, where President Trump feted Chinese leader Xi Jinping with military flyovers and at a lavish state dinner.
"Major countries should have special responsibilities for safeguarding international peace and security, and they should take the lead in complying with the rules, upholding rule of law, and doing what's right," Han said.
"China holds that the sovereignty and security of countries in the Middle East, including the Gulf, should be respected," he added.

President Donald Trump announced Friday that he is seeking to cancel almost $1 billion in federal funding, sidestepping congressional approval and earning criticism from lawmakers on both sides of the aisle.
Using a controversial move known as a “pocket rescission,” Trump said he wanted to nullify $810 million in spending that Congress had approved for programs and agencies, much of which would serve immigrants, minorities, and children.
Read More: A Debt Ceiling Fight Looms in 2027. Could a Democratic Congress Make it the Last One?
Over half of the cuts would land on the Health and Human Services (HHS) Department’s Office of Refugee Resettlement, according to a request sent to House Speaker Mike Johnson on Friday. It said that rescinding the funds is “consistent with the Administration's goal of ending the use of Federal taxpayer dollars to support non-citizens, putting Americans first.”
In a statement accompanying the request, the Trump Administration also called the funds “wasteful” and “harmful.”
The Government Accountability Office (GAO), a nonpartisan government watchdog, has asserted, however, that the move is an illegal sidestepping of the constitutionally protected separation of powers—chiefly, Congress's power of the purse.
A “pocket rescission” is not a formal or legal term; it was coined to reference a “ pocket veto ,” a process in which a bill fails to become law because the President does not sign it within 10 days and Congress’s adjournment prevents its return. Similarly, the “pocket rescission” aims to withdraw allocated funding without direct congressional intervention.
The timing is important when it comes to pocket rescissions. In order to be fully effective, this “occurs when a president asks Congress to rescind (or cancel) funds very close to the end of the fiscal year—so close that the funds expire before they can be used for new obligations,” according to the U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO).
The Office of Management and Budget (OMB), helmed by Director Russell Vought, submitted the requests Friday and holds that the move is valid under the 1974 Impoundment Control Act (ICA).
The Impoundment Control Act was created in response to President Richard Nixon’s heavy use of impoundments to achieve his policy goals. It has since been used to limit or regulate a president’s ability to control spending that has already been appropriated by building in 45 days of continuous congressional session. During this time, Congress is meant to review a President’s rescission requests and either approve them or see the funds released as planned.
Trump’s request to cancel $810 million in funding, however, came just five days before the end of the fiscal year on Sept. 30, all but ensuring that Congress will not have time to review the proposal in full or prevent the cuts from going into effect.
It is not the first time Trump has used this strategy to thwart spending attempts. He submitted a request on Aug. 28, 2025, to cancel $4.9 billion in foreign aid funds approved by Congress, including $3.2 billion that had been allocated to USAID . Although the move was contested, the Supreme Court last year stayed a lower court injunction requiring roughly $4 billion covered by the rescission request to be obligated.
The GAO claims that the move is illegal, writing on its website that this application of the ICA would “cede Congress’s power of the purse by allowing a president to, in effect, change the law by shortening the period of availability for fixed-period funds.”
“If Congress wanted a president to have that authority, it would need to change the law,” it continues.
Zachary Price, a professor at the University of California College of the Law, San Francisco, says that the move is an “abuse” of the ICA.
“It’s perverse to read that as, instead, creating this mechanism for unilaterally canceling funds,” Price tells TIME, adding that this interpretation is not supported by a lot of “historical practice.”
The maneuver seeks to withhold the funds until they expire at the end of the fiscal year, leaving Congress little time to respond.
In this case, Price says, it further showcases how the ICA is being manipulated.
The government “shouldn't have a lot of money left over at the end of the fiscal year if you've been spending it as you go in the way the statute contemplates,” he says.
He also points out that the American government is distinctly separated into three branches, with Congress, sitting in the legislative branch, being given the power to pass legislation—or, in this case, cancel funds that have already been appropriated. It has been explicitly separated from the authority of the executive branch and the President.
Bobby Kogan, the senior director of federal budget policy at the Center for American Progress, says it even plainer than Price: “The administration has picked a bunch of things that they hate, and they say, ‘Well, we're just not going to do those.’”
The Supreme Court’s intervention last year did not constitute a ruling on the authority of pocket rescissions, meaning that the Trump Administration's latest use of the tactic could face new legal challenges.
The largest portion of this year’s proposed cuts will target HHS programs providing nonprofit services for refugees and unaccompanied minors. Trump’s request would withdraw $567 million from those services.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) was also impacted, with a request to cancel funding for nonprofits that provide mental health services and social services to migrants. Another cut targets almost $25 million that had been slated for the Department of Education’s Special Programs for Migrant Students.
The Housing and Urban Development Department’s housing counseling services are also named amid the rescissions; the Trump Administration said that the program included non-governmental organizations with “divisive and DEI-centric agendas.”
The Trump Administration also aims to cancel $15 million from a Department of Justice office that focuses on reducing racial tensions, in addition to $10 million that had been allocated to the Minority Business Development Agency, which supports minority entrepreneurs.
“I assume that they're picking money to cancel based on some political calculus about what they can get away with,” Price says. When looking at the bigger picture, he argues this is just one maneuver in several to “establish stronger executive control over spending.”
The move also risks future negotiations in Congress, Price says. He explains that this application of the ICA would make it harder for Democrats and Republicans to compromise over spending if they anticipate that the sitting President will simply swoop in and cancel funding after thoughtful agreements have been reached.
“If the executive branch can come in and effectively impose a more kind of party line view of the spending, then you know why would people agree to the package in the first place?” he asks.
The rescission has earned blowback from both Republican and Democratic lawmakers who believe that the move sidesteps Congress's authority.
Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, the chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, lambasted the move on social media Friday evening , saying she would “work with my colleagues to address these illegal actions.”

articles.title_zh: Mother of woman found hanging in tree shocked as police say body was staged
articles.content_orig:
Tasia Fortune, a 29-year-old mother of four, was found hanging from a tree in August
Warning: This story contains distressing details
The mother of a woman found hanging in a tree in Mississippi has spoken of her shock after authorities said they believed her daughter was dead before her body was placed at the allegedly "staged" crime scene.
Tasia Fortune, a 29-year-old mother of four, was found hanging from a tree at an abandoned home in Jackson in August.
The discovery sparked widespread fears in the majority-black city because of the state's deep history of racial violence and lynchings. But on Friday, police said that Fortune had been dead before her body was hanged from the tree.
"I have more questions now than what I did before," her mother Christy Spivey told the BBC.
The Jackson Police Department said that the medical examiner who conducted Fortune's post-mortem examination had determined that her death was a homicide and that "the scene and the hanging were staged ".
Officials have not disclosed the exact cause of death or shared any potential motive behind the allegedly staged hanging.
Three people have been arrested in the case, all of whom are black.
"I was hoping to be more relieved," Spivey said, adding that the police had not specified how the three suspects were connected to her daughter - or why her death was allegedly staged in this way.
"Still no cause of death, no date of death - nothing," she said. "What actually killed her?"
Fortune's death left the local community on edge and lawmakers demanding federal probes . But the latest developments have created more confusion.
Christy Spivey told the BBC she was upset at how the police had handled the investigation
Spivey told the BBC that getting the update from the coroner that her daughter did not die by hanging initially gave her peace - at least her daughter did not die in such a gruesome manner, she thought.
"When the police called me, I started crying and thanked them and felt a little more at peace than I had before," she said. "I just hope they've got the right person/people."
When the latest details surrounding her death emerged this week, she said she was "starting to break down".
Police told a court on Friday that Fortune's death was thought to be as a result of a drug-related dispute. A detective said Fortune may have been killed over allegations she stole drugs.

By CHRIS MELORE, US DEPUTY SCIENCE EDITOR
Published: 10:00 EDT, 26 September 2026 | Updated: 11:00 EDT, 26 September 2026
Hurricane Nolo is expected to cause 'catastrophic flooding' as the life-threatening storm nears the Hawaiian islands and over one million Americans this weekend.
A state of emergency has already been issued in Hawaii and forecasters now believe the strengthening hurricane could bring historic levels of rainfall, particularly across the Big Island (also known as Hawaii Island).
AccuWeather forecasters warned that the week-long deluge could dump as much as 55 inches of rain on the Big Island - just under five feet of precipitation.
If that prediction is correct, Nolo would be the second wettest hurricane in Hawaii's history, falling just behind Hurricane Lane's 58 inches in 2018.
The National Hurricane Center (NHC) said in a statement: 'Life-threatening, catastrophic flooding and mudslides are possible, especially in areas of steep terrain across the eastern and southern portions of the Big Island and Maui.'
Local officials on the islands have also urged residents and tourists to be prepared to evacuate flood-prone areas as the hurricane makes its closest approach.
Although Nolo is not projected to make landfall, AccuWeather has projected that at least two to four inches of rain will fall across the entire island chain. The hurricane is currently about 140 miles from Hawaii.
Both Maui and the Big Island are also expected to be struck by dangerous and sustained wind gusts reaching between 60 and 80 mph through Monday.
Hurricane Nolo is expected to become a Category 4 hurricane this weekend with winds over 130 mph
Residents in Hawaii began preparing for potentially catastrophic flooding this week
Nolo erupted into a tropical storm on Wednesday less than 400 miles south of the Hawaiian islands and has been slowly gaining strength throughout the week.
AccuWeather and NHC have both warned that Nolo will likely reach major hurricane status by Saturday afternoon, growing into a Category 3 storm with sustained winds exceeding 111 mph.
Saturday is expected to be the peak of the threat for Hawaii, as the hurricane makes its closest approach to land.
The worst of the rain and possible hurricane-force winds are expected to hit the exposed slopes of the Big Island's eastern side. Forecasts have predicted that this side of the island will see at least two feet of rain.
Maui, a major tourist destination just 30 miles to the west of the Big Island, will also see increasing rain and possible tropical storm conditions on Saturday, as winds range between 40 and 60 mph.
Mayor Richard Bissen of Maui County said in a statement : 'During this above-normal hurricane season, recent storms remind us that we cannot afford to be complacent.'
'Our top priority is the safety of our community. Now is the time for all of us to review household emergency plans, check supplies and make sure you can receive important alerts and information.'
National Weather Service officials in Honolulu warned: 'Leave immediately if evacuation orders are given for your area.'
Hurricane Lala caused at least two deaths and billions of dollars in damage from flooding and mudslides in August
Forecasters have warned that more than three feet of rain could fall on Hawaii's Big Island
A prediction of 55 inches of rain by AccuWeather would make Hurricane Nolo the second wettest hurricane in Hawaii's history
Hawaii's Big Island is home to more than 200,000 people, and the island is still recovering from the devastating effects of Hurricanes Lala and Lowell this summer.
The storm destroyed over 100 homes, damaged hundreds more and killed at least five people across the state, with the heaviest damage occurring on the Big Island during Lala's approach on August 15.
Downpours, flooding and mudslides, similar to what is expected during Nolo, led to more than 100 homes on the Big Island being washed away during the August hurricane.
Hurricane Lowell struck the opposite end of the island chain in September, causing widespread power outages and property damage on the islands of Kauaʻi and Niʻihau.
Emergency shelters have been opened on the Big Island ahead of the hurricane's arrival.
Hawaii County Mayor Kimo Alameda said in a statement: 'If your home flooded before, or is at risk, consider moving to safer shelter before the full force of the storm hits. Because the ground remains saturated, flooding may happen rapidly.'
By Sunday, Nolo is expected to start moving away from Hawaii, although the hurricane will likely continue strengthening, growing into a Category 4 storm with winds surpassing 130 mph.
Rain and flooding will likely continue before gradually easing heading into the new week.

articles.title_orig: Boeing flags 737 Max software glitch affecting some automated approach functions
articles.title_zh: Boeing flags 737 Max software glitch affecting some automated approach functions
articles.content_orig:
Boeing said it flagged a software glitch last month on some 737 Max aircraft that could affect certain landing procedures, as the manufacturer seeks federal approval for the fourth and final model in its best-selling aircraft family.
The Federal Aviation Administration said Saturday that it is assessing the problem and "will take immediate action if it identifies a safety concern" and that it will review Boeing's proposed fix.
Boeing said the issue could arise after a missed approach when pilots alter a preprogrammed flight path, and that pilots must take additional steps to use automated tools on subsequent approaches.
"We shared information with operators that reinforced existing pilot procedures for safely handling such cases. Our engineers are working on a software update to permanently address the issue," Boeing said. The Wall Street Journal reported the issue earlier.
The company said that pilots are trained to land without the automated system. "We are working directly with airlines to formalize a procedure that will allow pilots to reenable automated vertical navigation should this situation occur," Boeing said.
U.S. airlines told CNBC that they do not have Max 8 and Max 9 airplanes with the updated software tied to the glitch in their fleets. Airlines can revert some Maxes to the older software version.
All-Boeing 737 Max carrier Southwest Airlines said it is "aware of the issue and is engaged with Boeing and the FAA."
It added that "none of our fleet is equipped with Version U.14, including new deliveries of Max 8 airplanes." United Airlines also said it's not taking any Max aircraft deliveries with the new software.
However, questions remain about the two other models, the Max 7 and Max 10. The Federal Aviation Administration certified the Max 7 , the smallest of the Max family, in early August with the newest software installed. It wasn't immediately clear if the aircraft could be delivered or fly with an older version of software.
Additionally, Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg told investors earlier this month that he expected FAA certification of the Max 10 "very soon."
"We have been engaged with Boeing and the FAA and will continue to work closely with both as they evaluate this matter and determine next steps," Alaska Airlines , a Max 10 customer, said Saturday.
The issue comes after years of delays of Boeing's Max planes following safety and manufacturing crises, including the two deadly crashes of Max 8 aircraft in 2018 and 2019 that killed 346 people. A flawed flight control software system — which has since been updated — was implicated in both crashes.
There are 2,430 Max aircraft currently in service globally, according to Cirium.

Carrot Top rose to fame in the 1990s for his curly red mane and loud wardrobe, and has remained  a pop culture figure for decades.

Two companies now say they will accept advertising for director Alex Gibney’s upcoming documentary about Elon Musk, following earlier reporting that a number of social media platforms had rejected the ads.
The Hollywood Reporter published a story Friday saying that TikTok, Meta, YouTube, and X had all refused to run paid ads promoting the trailer for “Musk.”
However, when TechCrunch reached out to Meta on Saturday, a spokesperson said, “This was an error and the ads are being restored.” We’ve asked Meta for more details and will update this article if we hear back.
YouTube also posted an update Saturday , noting that “the trailer has always been available on YouTube.” (Indeed, that’s how we were able embed it at the end of this article.) The company added, “When submitted as an ad, it was temporarily restricted by our system. Following review the ad has been cleared to run.”
X’s rejection is unsurprising — Musk, who owns the social media platform, recently posted that “Dogshit is worth more respect than Gibney.”
But Meta, TikTok, and YouTube reportedly rejected the ad for “political content,” which the platforms have various restrictions on. (Meta said last year that it will stop accepting political ads in the European Union , while TikTok says it doesn’t run them at all .) It’s not clear how a documentary trailer counts as campaign advertising, and the film’s U.S. distributor Bleecker Street told the Hollywood Reporter that it had appealed the rejections.
Gibney has directed acclaimed documentaries including “Going Clear” (about the Church of Scientology) and “The Inventor” (about Elizabeth Holmes and Theranos), as well as a movie about Steve Jobs . “Musk,” his latest, premiered at the Venice International Film Festival earlier this month and has received almost universally positive reviews . The film currently has a 100% “fresh” rating on Rotten Tomatoes and is set for theatrical release in the United States on October 9.
Vulture’s Bilge Ebiri described the nearly four-hour documentary as a revealing look at Musk’s tech career, his alliance with President Donald Trump, and his personal life, with interview subjects including ex-wife Justine Musk and former right-wing influencer Ashley St. Clair (who recently had a child with Musk but now describes him as “a nuke”).
Ebiri wrote that while the film is a “fascinating” character study, adding, “As a tale of modern business, it’s revealing. And as a warning about our future, it’s terrifying.”
Despite the initial wave of critical acclaim, The Hollywood Reporter also said that Universal Pictures was wavering in its commitment to distribute the film internationally, reportedly due to the studio’s fear of angering the Trump administration. articles.title_orig: Pope Leo celebrates open-air mass before 700,000 people in Paris
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo celebrates open-air mass before 700,000 people in Paris
articles.content_orig:
Crowds line Place de la Concorde on second day of pontiff’s first official papal visit to France in 18 years
Hundreds of thousands of people lined the Avenue des Champs-Élysées in ⁠Paris on Saturday to attend an open-air mass with Pope Leo, on the second day of his visit to France .
The Vatican estimated 700,000 people turned out for the outdoor mass with the 71-year-old American pope – about 100,000 more than the number of people who had registered to attend.
It took place at the Place de la Concorde, the site of bloody executions by guillotine during the French Revolution – when Louis XVI’s staunchly Catholic rule was overthrown – and now the centre of the secular republic.
The choice of the site, a symbol of the French republic to many, was criticised by supporters of France’s strict legislation separating church and state in public life.
But cheers rang out in the crowd as the pope thanked ‌God in his homily for the chance to ‌visit France on a whirlwind four-day, three-city tour to promote Catholicism and its teachings.
It is the first official papal visit to France in 18 years.
Pope Leo asked those in the crowd not to keep their faith to themselves. “Let it overflow, so that those you meet may be refreshed and their thirst satisfied,” he said. “From this beautiful city of Paris, I pray fervently that the living water of the Holy Spirit may flow throughout France.”
He told Catholics that only their faith, and not material things, can provide true happiness.
“Only God can fill the emptiness within us,” he said.
The security zone for the event – the biggest of the papal tour – stretched about 1.4 miles (2.2km), shutting down road traffic in central Paris from the Place de la Concorde to the Arc de Triomphe and beyond.
Chanting “Leo, Leo” and “Long live the pope”, crowds of people waved French and Vatican flags as the pontiff rode slowly down the grand boulevard of the Champs-Élysées aboard a popemobile – a specially designed, partly open vehicle used during public appearances.
He stopped frequently along the way as babies were lifted out of the crowd and brought to him to receive a papal caress on their heads. The city centre was sealed off for the service, with helicopters circling overhead and snipers positioned on rooftops.
About 14,500 police officers, gendarmes, military personnel and firefighters were deployed to the event, which was attended by 2,400 priests and deacons, and about 100 bishops.
Marie-Élisabeth, a 44-year-old nun from Burgundy, told a reporter for France 24: “This event is a way for us to say loud and proud that Christians are here.”
Speaking to reporters from Agence France-Presse, Sylvie Leclerc, a 51-year-old teacher, also said she and her fellow Christians want to share their fervour for their faith. “You don’t hear much from us Catholics, but now we’re going to make some noise!” she said. “But to proclaim love, peace, joy.”

articles.title_orig: Russia expected to intensify hybrid war on Europe
articles.title_zh: Russia expected to intensify hybrid war on Europe
articles.content_orig:
Just a few months ago, Russia's war was an distant reality for many people in Europe outside of Ukraine. If Russian drones occasionally entered the airspace of countries like Poland or Romania, even official statements seemed strangely dismissive and abstract. Even after a Russian drone struck a high-rise apartment building in the eastern Romanian city of Galati in late May this year, many EU and NATO representatives hesitated to accuse Russia of intentional action. At most, there was discussion of hybrid warfare.
The situation has changed radically since the summer. Drone overflights have become almost daily in certain parts of central and southeastern Europe, and there have even been crashes and explosions, particularly in countries bordering Ukraine. Alerts are becoming more frequent, with authorities increasingly having to close airspace or suspend operations at airports, as unauthorized flights are detected. Russia has been bombing border crossings, infrastructure and trains in Ukraine, but very close to other borders. Acts of sabotage are also increasingly common.
For the Baltic states, Poland , Moldova and Romania in particular, the war has long ceased to be "hybrid." More and more, politicians in these countries are saying that Russia is acting deliberately.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
This became evident this week in an unprecedented manner. Moldova recorded four drones entering Moldovan airspace, two of which exploded in Moldovan territory. Wreckage of another was also found. The country's northern airspace was closed temporarily. Two drones also violated Romanian airspace; with one crashing near the northern town of Solca. A nearby border crossing with Ukraine a few dozen kilometers away was closed as a result. NATO aircraft were scrambled near the Danube Delta.
The scrambling of NATO aircraft has become more common in response to Russian air attacks in Ukraine.
In Poland, NATO fighter jets were scrambled twice in response to Russian attacks near the border with Ukraine. Two Polish border crossings were evacuated after a fire broke out at a Starlink ground station near the village of Wola Krobowska , 40 kilomters (ca. 25 miles) south of the Polish capital Warsaw, on Wednesday night. The station is used to route internet traffic through Poland to Ukraine.
On the same day, a Russian Mi-8 helicopter violated Polish airspace and remained there for 42 seconds according to the Polish military.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk spoke very bluntly in Krakow on Thursday and said that Russia was refining its "disgusting forms of pressure" and Poland must be prepared for them.
Russian President Vladimir Putin "wants to exhaust Ukraine by destroying its industrial and energy infrastructure, but he also wants to exhaust Europe," Tusk said. He added that there was a suspicion that the fire at the Starlink ground station had been deliberate.
Earlier this month, Tusk had already warned the Polish parliament that there might be Russian drone and even missile attacks against those who supported Ukraine.
Moldovan President Maia Sandu also reacted very strongly on Thursday, saying that Russia's war was a danger to all of Europe and reasserting Moldova's support for Ukraine.
In Romania , reactions were less clear. Defense Minister Radu Miruta said that not more than a "diplomatic protest" was needed, though he acknowledged that the drone that had crashed in Solca had new technical features, which suggested it could be a newer type of Russian jet-powered drone. In New York on Wednesday, in his address to the United Nations General Assembly , Romanian President Nicusor Dan had said: "We are in the fifth year of the illegal, unprovoked and unjustified war of aggression waged on a large scale against Ukraine by a permanent member of the Security Council." He had added that as the "EU member state with the longest border with Ukraine, Romania has directly felt the effects of this war through repeated violations of our airspace."
And he too reasserted support for Ukraine: "We have said it before, and we say it again: Romania will stand with Ukraine and its people, who are acting in legitimate self-defense, for as long as it takes."
Meanwhile, there is growing speculation that Russia could expand its war to Western Europe. On Thursday, the Spanish newspaper El Mundo published information about a CIA report warning that Russia could be preparing drone attacks on Italy , France and Spain . The attacks could be launched from international waters in the Mediterranean and from vessels that were part of Russia's shadow fleet.
There has been no official confirmation so far. French President Emmanuel Macron said that that the CIA had not informed France of this information, but he did say that the possibility Russia could launch an attack against Europe was "plausible."
At a press conference in Denmark on Thursday, politicians and military officials warned that Russia was expected to intensify its hybrid war against the West and NATO in the coming months. The situation is currently the most serious since the end of the Cold War," said Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus.

articles.title_orig: Security lapses at Utah campus where Charlie Kirk was killed, review says
articles.title_zh: Security lapses at Utah campus where Charlie Kirk was killed, review says
articles.content_orig:
An independent review has pointed to a number of security shortcomings at the Utah campus where conservative activist Charlie Kirk was shot dead last year.
The report said Utah Valley University (UVU) did not carry out a proper written security assessment nor prepare an event action plan, deferring key decision-making about the event to Kirk's conservative organisation Turning Point USA.
It also said that Kirk's aides had insisted on a outdoor venue, overriding security concerns from campus officials, who then failed to properly assess the dangers.
The 31-year-old activist had been addressing thousands of people in an Orem campus courtyard when he was shot from a nearby rooftop on 10 September 2025.
Kirk's family said the report reinforced their concerns about how the event was managed.
University officials had raised concerns in August 2025 about holding the event at a location surrounded by tall buildings and had suggested alternative venues, including some indoors, the report - published by UVU - says.
"But a Turning Point representative insisted that Kirk speak at a campus courtyard because he had been there previously and the organisation was familiar with the location," it adds.
Despite the "significant protective operations considerations", no line-of-sight assessment was documented in the planning process, the external consultants note.
They also identified shortcomings in the co-ordination between university police and Kirk's private security team.
A proposed meeting between the university's police chief and Turning Point security shortly before the event did not take place, the report said.
The reviewers described the absence of a joint security briefing and walk-through as a missed opportunity to have identified risks, clarified responsibilities and considered additional security measures.
However, the review concluded that no university employee or representative had acted in bad faith or shown "willful and wanton disregard" for anyone's safety.
Kirk's family has previously accused the university of serious security failures and has filed a wrongful-death notice , a step that can precede legal action.
The family's lawyer, Brett Parkinson, said the independent report released on Friday backed up the concerns raised by Kirk's loved ones.
"The buck stopped with UVU leadership and law enforcement," Parkinson said in a statement to the Associated Press. "Justice for Charlie and his family requires true accountability for UVU's fatal shortcomings that day."
When asked for comment on the findings, Turning Point USA referred to Parkinson's statement.
The review makes numerous recommendations aimed at improving security for major campus events.
UVU President Jon Anderson said the university must "learn from the findings of this review, and follow through on its recommendations".
It has previously been reported that the campus police failed to conduct security procedures that are common practice at US high-profile events, including flying a drone to monitor rooftops or security screening like bag checks and metal detectors.
Kirk had been debating UVU students about US mass shootings, as part of a series of events across different university campuses, when he was shot in the neck shortly after noon. He was rushed to hospital but later pronounced dead.
His alleged killer, Tyler Robinson, has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder in connection with Kirk's death. Prosecutors are seeking the death penalty.

articles.title_orig: Rogue OpenAI agents targeted three separate US government websites
articles.title_zh: Rogue OpenAI agents targeted three separate US government websites
articles.content_orig:
OpenAI said Friday that some of its AI agents went rogue and probed US government websites this summer — the latest revelation of the artificial intelligence company’s technology.
The New York Times first reported that the AI agents went rogue and attempted to gain access to the Education Department, the Commerce Department and the Securities and Exchange Commission, according to security researchers at AI research lab Transluce.
OpenAI said Saturday that its agents accessed publicly available data from the Commerce Department’s Census Bureau using login credentials it found online, and separately shared public data from the SEC website on another website. OpenAI’s agents attempted but failed to gain access to the Education Department and gather data from its civil rights office, according to the report.
OpenAI told CNN in an email that it notified the agencies of the findings while continuing an “extensive review of misaligned model activity.”
“Most of the activity we’ve reviewed so far involved routine research tasks, such as accessing public web content to answer questions. Some involved government websites because our models often turn to them as authoritative sources of public information,” the spokesperson said.
The Commerce Department, SEC and Education Department did not immediately respond to CNN’s requests for comment.
Rep. Jay Obernolte, the Republican co-chair of the AI caucus, told CNN’s Anderson Cooper on Friday that the incident is “another example of a loss of human control.”
“We need to align the values that these models are trained on with human values, and if we can do that, we can get these models to conform to our standards for human behavior,” he said.
The report comes just days after Australia’s prime minister said that an OpenAI agent hacked into the country’s national healthcare database, marking the first known case of AI hacking a government network. Transluce on Wednesday said that it had detected AI agents going rogue dating back to at least March, unsuccessfully targeting a University of New Mexico library and the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare site.
The Australian website probe occurred in June, an OpenAI spokesperson previously told CNN, but the company was only made aware of it in August.
OpenAI has been investigating agents’ use of internet access since the breach of AI start-up Hugging Face in July.
Sam Altman, OpenAI’s chief executive, said Friday on social media site X that the company was not “as fast as we would have liked.”
“We are trying to balance our desire for transparency with gaining a clear understanding … Hugging Face is still the most severe event we’ve seen,” he wrote .
Competitors Anthropic , Meta and Google have also reported that their agents have gone rogue during breach attempts.
Such breaches have raised alarms within the artificial intelligence community. Tech leaders have jointly called for a slowdown of the technology’s development following Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s essay about “ pacing the frontier ” in mid-September. Amodei warned that people may lose control of AI, which could be misused for “cyberattacks and bioterrorism.”
During the United Nations’ General Assembly on Wednesday, Amodei and Altman urged the UN Security Council to set international standards. Altman said countries need accurate and speedy reporting so that the “world can learn from failures before they become catastrophes.”
Amodei’s warning followed a former Anthropic researcher, Jacob Coxon, whose viral post on X called out AI companies for not acting responsibly with the technology’s development and warned that it “will kill us all.”
AI “doomerism” has faced pushback from tech leaders like Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who said there’s a “0% chance” of the world coming to an end in 2030.
CNN’s Hadas Gold, Hilary Whiteman and Max Saltman contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Olivia Rodrigo’s Dress Literally Melts Off Her Body on Stage in a Moment of Fashion Magic
articles.title_zh: Olivia Rodrigo’s Dress Literally Melts Off Her Body on Stage in a Moment of Fashion Magic
articles.content_orig:
Olivia Rodrigo has always understood the art of a good fashion reference and a costume change. On the GUTs tour, she had a rotation of slogan tees for the encore that changed from city to city. Her “ drop dead ” music video was jam-packed with sartorial tributes to Sofia Coppola and Jane Birkin. Styled by Chloe and Chenelle Delgadillo, she’s established an on-stage wardrobe rooted in riot grrrl-esque aesthetics and romantic shapes.
On the opening night of The Unraveled Tour , though, Rodrigo swerved the backstage quick-change, wearing a dress that transformed while she was still wearing it. Performing “The Cure” at Hartford’s PeoplesBank Arena on September 25, she appeared in a pristine white collared mini dress with a sweet pleated skirt. Then, as the song reached its climax and Rodrigo repeated, “ I’m unraveled, I’m unraveled ...,” artificial rain began to pour from above. The white outer layer started to disintegrate before the audience’s eyes, eventually washing away to reveal a fire-red corseted bodysuit and miniskirt underneath—a pleasingly literal interpretation of the tour’s title.
The piece was custom-designed and developed by Hussein Chalayan, and revisits one of the designer’s most memorable runway experiments. For his spring 2016 collection , two models stood motionless in white, military-inflected paper garments before hidden showerheads suddenly released water overhead. Their outer layers dissolved, exposing palm-patterned dresses underneath, punctuated with Swarovski crystals. Chalayan and his team had spent around six months developing the water-reactive material.
For Chalayan, clothing has rarely been a static proposition. The Cyprus-born British designer built his career around garments that move, mutate, disappear, and occasionally seem to defy their own material limits. His Central Saint Martins graduate collection famously included clothes that had first been buried underground and left to decay; later came dresses incorporating mechanical parts, lasers, LEDs, and crystal “pollen,” as well as his now-iconic fall 2000 coffee table that transformed into a wooden skirt. Transformation was not a runway gimmick but a recurring cadence in dialogue with design. His work finds a means of using technology, engineering, and performance to ask what a garment might be capable of beyond simply clothing the body.
The now-iconic fall 2000 coffee table that transformed into a wooden skirt.
The remote control spring 2000 dress.
The spring 2016 melting dresses were a particularly distilled expression of Chalayan’s codes. Inspired by Cuba and its changing political and cultural landscape, Chalayan imagined severe uniform-like shells washing away to expose new possibilities. “I liked the idea of a garment that could melt and reveal something else underneath,” he said at the time . Nearly 11 years later, Rodrigo has given the concept a second life: where Chalayan used dissolution to express transformation, she deploys it as pop spectacle, making the very idea of becoming “unraveled” happen in real time.
Olivia Rodrigo’s tour wardrobe has otherwise stuck to the pretty, grungy, vintage-inflected vocabulary she has made her own. There was a white ruffled babydoll dress by Dilara Findikoglu; a cropped graphic T-shirt with hot-pink micro shorts; a flared leather mini from R&M Leathers; and a tank top worn with vintage blue jeans and Vans.
The Hartford dates mark the opening two nights of Rodrigo’s new tour—expect moments of major fashion history, imbued with Rodrigo’s own personal storytelling, to continue unfurling.

articles.title_orig: Anger grows across Spain after elderly woman evicted from her home of 70 years
articles.title_zh: Anger grows across Spain after elderly woman evicted from her home of 70 years
articles.content_orig:
An 87-year-old Spanish woman was forcibly evicted Wednesday from the Madrid apartment she had lived in for more than 70 years, in a case that highlights a growing housing crisis in the country.
Video showed Maricarmen Abascal, who is a wheelchair user, being taken out of the building in the Spanish capital’s Retiro neighborhood on a stretcher and driven away in an ambulance.
Hundreds of supporters had gathered outside the building overnight to protest her eviction, with dozens of police officers holding them back as some tried to stop the eviction from going ahead. In a social media video posted Friday by the Madrid tenants union, Abascal gave thanks for the support she had received.
Abascal’s lawyer, Beatriz Duro, described the force used in the eviction as “completely disproportionate and unnecessary” and decried the intransigence of the building’s owners.
The case has brought new attention to an ongoing housing crisis in major cities across Spain, as gentrification has caused rents to skyrocket and the stock of affordable housing to shrink, leading to growing public anger.
Tenants unions and other housing groups on Thursday held protests and rallies in 16 cities, including Granada, Logroño and Zaragoza. The Madrid tenants union plans to hold another major protest in the capital Saturday evening.
An investment fund acquired Abascal’s building in 2018 and sought a steep increase in her rent, and she had been fighting eviction for more than five years, according to the Madrid tenants union.
Duro said court officials and representatives of the fund, Urbagestión, had refused to suspend the eviction despite a pending court filing, humanitarian appeals and evidence that public authorities were working to secure alternative accommodation.
“They’re all inhumane,” Abascal said in a Spanish television interview the day before her eviction. “It’s as if I’m living with a machete at the back of my neck, ready to be chopped off at any moment.”
Duro also said an anonymous individual had offered to cover the rent payments, but the landlord declined to sign a new lease.
“We’ve been trying to negotiate with the landlords right up until the last moment, and they’ve flatly refused everything,” she said, decrying “a lack of humanity” in her treatment and “all these public resources” channeled into enabling the eviction.
Urbagestión did not respond to a request for comment.
The fresh wave of anger comes after protests in recent years against overtourism in Barcelona, where activists say a surge in apartments being used for short-term vacation rentals has contributed to a shortage of affordable housing.
The European Union announced new rules earlier this month aimed at tackling the housing crunch caused by short-term rentals in tourism hot spots.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez described the eviction as “a social tragedy that we cannot accept either as a country or, of course, from the perspective of public institutions.”
Speaking at the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Wednesday, Sánchez accused Madrid’s conservative regional government of pursuing luxury penthouses while ignoring demand for social housing.
Irene Hernández López, a 31-year-old test engineer living and renting in Chamberí, about 2 miles from Retiro, said what had happened to Abascal was “outrageous,” and she is worried similar evictions were already happening to other tenants around the city.
“Housing has become a product that people do business with,” she told NBC News. “It no longer matters that it’s your personal world, where you live and where you do your life.”
Hernández López, who pays 500 euros ($570) for a room in an apartment she shares with two others, said she was currently looking to move because the property was old and needs repairs, but that the rental market in Madrid was “terrible,” with prices “rising extremely quickly” and very little available.
“Some rooms are 500 euros or 600 euros and you think, ‘How am I supposed to live here? How can I pay 500 euros for this?’” she said. “I do think prices should be regulated, because wages aren’t going up while housing prices keep increasing. I don’t know how we’re supposed to keep going.”
Dan Nicander, secretary-general for the International Union of Tenants, said the situation in Spain was something his organization had seen in many countries in Europe.
“It’s a part of the financialization problem, seeing housing as an asset more than a home to people,” he told NBC News.
It’s “really tough” for the people living in the houses to do anything about it, he added, saying the responsibility lay with  politicians “to regulate the market in a way that it shouldn’t be that easy to buy and invest and then not [be] using the houses as homes.”
“Housing is a right,” he said. “It’s a fundamental right, first and foremost. It shouldn’t be a commodity.”
Jamie Gray is a senior desk editor for NBC News based in London.
Freddie Clayton is a freelance journalist based in London.

President Donald Trump lashed out over his press coverage again Saturday morning after a federal judge ordered him to immediately lift a White House ban on CNN, Politico and MS NOW.
In two early morning Truth Social posts, Trump questioned why journalists should have access to the “very sacred” White House. The posts came shortly after his administration barred CNN from Air Force One Saturday and replaced the outlet with LindellTV for his trip to Knoxville, Tennessee, to attend a college football game.
“Why should perpetrators of FAKE NEWS, like CNN and MSDNC, be allowed access to a very sacred place, the White House?” Trump demanded. “Despite my big Election Win, almost 100% of ‘TRUMP’ coverage is negative, and has been for years!”
Less than two hours later, Trump escalated his criticism.
“FAKE NEWS SHOULD NOT BE ALLOWED IN THE WHITE HOUSE!!! IT HAS GONE ON FAR TOO LONG, AT A TREMENDOUS COST TO OUR COUNTRY,” he wrote.
The latest clash with the media began September 18, when Trump abruptly announced that CNN, MS NOW and Politico would be barred from the White House . According to reports, the ban came hours after his aide Natalie Harp showed him videos of unflattering news coverage.
“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” he wrote on Truth Social. “Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.”
By the following morning, CNN, MS NOW and Politico all said that their journalists had been stopped from accessing the White House grounds, with some reporters saying that they were asked to hand over their badges.
On September 21, the outlets filed a lawsuit against Trump and several of his top aides, arguing that the ban violates the Fifth Amendment’s Due Process Clause, as well as the First Amendment, and calls for the press passes to be restored.
“This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” the lawsuit states.
The Justice Department has argued that Trump has the authority to ban the outlets on “ national security ” grounds, claiming that “access to the White House is a privilege—not a right.”
On September 24, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ordered the Trump administration to temporarily reinstate the outlets’ press badges. By that afternoon, reporters regained access to the White House .
Yet, on September 25, the White House announced that CNN will not be allowed on Air Force One when Trump flies to Knoxville, Tennessee, on Saturday for a college football game, the network reported .
CNN is part of a rotating press pool that covers White House events for major TV networks.
Instead, the White House listed LindellTV, a conservative online video platform founded by Trump ally Mike Lindell , on the Air Force One Saturday schedule. Real America’s Voice was also listed.
“I love an open free press,” Trump told reporters Saturday morning before departing from the White House on Marine One.
“What I don’t like is fake news, and they’re fake news 100 percent,” he said, referring to the three outlets he banned. “In two years I doubt they did one good story.”
Trump has long had an extremely combative relationship with the press , accusing reporters of unfair and biased coverage, lobbing personal insults against them and insinuating that those he opposes should be punished.
The president previously curtailed The Associated Press from accessing certain presidential spaces in 2025 after the outlet continued using the “Gulf of Mexico” despite Trump rebranding it as the “Gulf of America.” In 2018, Trump also revoked CNN reporter Jim Acosta’s press pass following a contentious news conference.

“This move is a diplomatic all-timer,” Santi Ruiz, a policy-focused writer for the Institute for Progress and editorial team member at AI company Anthropic, posted on X. “It's like Messi cutting inside. You know it’s coming. It doesn’t matter how many times they run it. You’re getting those pandas, and you’ll like it.”
The tried-and-tested offering came once again on Thursday as Chinese President Xi Jinping announced during his state visit to the U.S. that Ping Ping and Fu Shuang , two giant pandas from a research base in Chengdu, would be lent to Zoo Atlanta in the state of Georgia—but whether this so-called panda diplomacy remains as welcome as it has over the decades is less clear, eliciting mixed reactions in 2026.
The practice gained traction after the National Zoo received giant pandas from Beijing in the wake of President Richard Nixon and First Lady Pat Nixon’s historic trip to China in 1972, which marked a new, positive chapter in U.S.-China relations.
China claims ownership of nearly all the giant pandas in the world, even their offspring, and controls who receives them. Beijing eventually shifted from gifting giant pandas to leasing them to other countries in 1984 as the animal’s population dwindled, but the practice continued and spread to other nations like Austria, Canada, and Malaysia. China regularly considers loaning pandas an act of goodwill—even when the host nation typically foots the bill of about $1 million annually for a pair.
A giant panda’s presence or absence in a country tends to represent ebbs and flows of its relationship with China. For instance, amid tensions with Japan over Taiwan , Tokyo returned two giant pandas to Sichuan on loan in January, marking the first time Japan does not have a giant panda since 1972, when China-Japan ties first normalized. In 2010, two U.S.-born panda cubs returned to China , days after Chinese officials warned then-President Barack Obama against meeting the Dalai Lama, whom Beijing considers a separatist.
“No other animal has been turned into a symbol to the extent that pandas have been,” says Czeslaw Tubilewicz, a senior lecturer at Adelaide University.
It’s also no coincidence that Zoo Atlanta received the giant pandas, Tubilewicz says, as the gift represented Beijing’s appreciation of Georgia’s historical economic partnership with China on several aspects: “When most southern states, especially Republican states, turned very negative on China, Georgia continued its pro-China policy consistently. So when it comes to those pandas, and in [Zoo Atlanta], in a way, Xi Jinping is trying to kill two birds with two pandas.”
But China’s transformation from a developing economy to one of the world’s superpowers has also raised questions about whether the gesture of sending giant pandas still works. China is massively different from how it used to be in the 1970s, and is currently embroiled in a wide range of issues, not only with the U.S., but also with other countries, which makes categorizing it neatly as a friend or foe less easy.
Ja Ian Chong, associate professor of political science at the National University of Singapore, tells TIME that “the image of the pandas as soft, friendly, and cuddly—they don’t work today because a lot of [China’s aggressive] actions now are a lot more visible and fresh in people’s minds.”
“No one cares about pandas when national security or geostrategic interests come into play,” Tubilewicz added.
A 2022 peer-reviewed study at the University of Connecticut found that U.S. students who viewed panda videos that were not sourced from the government were likely to have a positive attitude toward Chinese culture and, in turn, Chinese people.
But while China’s practice of leasing pandas gives some people warm feelings, it makes others hot with anger. Conservationists and animal advocates have argued against using pandas as geopolitical pawns. Following the South Korea-China Summit earlier this year, the countries’ respective environmental officials discussed additional giant panda loans. But a Korean animal rights group slammed the move , saying that the creatures “are not beings born for human entertainment or interstate friendship.”
And many others are also starting to look past the panda diplomacy and demand other measures. A 2026 survey of U.S. adults conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago found that 28% of respondents said sending pandas to American zoos would improve their view of China, but much higher percentages said that more concrete actions like Chinese cooperation on curbing fentanyl precursors or easing trade restrictions would improve their view of China.
“The symbolism was still dominant in the 1970s,” Chong said. “It’s just that, given the lack of information, given the environment of that time, the symbolism probably got a lot more traction before than today.”
While surveys show many Americans are warming to China , Chong says “deep reservoirs of reservations remain,” particularly among Trump’s MAGA base: a July survey from the Chicago Council on Global Affairs says that 63% of MAGA Republicans favor limiting the growth of Chinese power.
“Affection for pandas does not automatically translate into support for Chinese government policies,” Yu Tao, associate professor in Chinese Studies at the University of Western Australia, tells TIME. “Its more realistic contribution is to sustain public goodwill and opportunities for cooperation. The strongest case for panda diplomacy is that it gives people something they want to preserve in a relationship otherwise defined pretty much by disputes.”
